children: By Johann M Cherian and Niket Nishant

Most Latin American currencies and equities fell on Tuesday, with Colombia's peso leading losses as worries about the country's fiscal outlook battered the currency, while Brazilian assets were poised to end a three-day slide on optimism over fiscal consolidation.
Concerns over deteriorating public finances in regional economies, coupled with a stronger dollar on US Federal Reserve rate hike expectations, have pressured Latin American assets this year.
Barring the Colombian peso, all major regional currencies are on track for sharp annual losses and MSCI's equities benchmark (.MILA00000PUS) is on track for a 5% drop this year.

declined 3% to breach the 3,600-per-dollar mark for the first time since June and was on track to mark its fifth straight day of losses. However, it was still up 4% for the year, aided by gains earlier in the year on higher prices of oil — a top export item.

Tuesday's losses were tied to uncertainties over a tax law, dubbed the 'Rescue Law,' that was debated in Congress. Revenue-generating food taxes were rejected along with other changes, risking potential failure of the bill and further deterioration of public finances.

slipped 1.3% to its May 2025 low after data showed a closely watched core inflation measure eased unexpectedly. The country's central bank, which targets inflation at 3% plus or minus one percentage point, is expected to keep rates unchanged next month.
Uncertainty over Mexico's trade relations with the US has been an overhang for its assets this year. However, hopes are high for a thaw in trade tensions next year.

"Trade negotiations were difficult. We need to wait a little because in January the Democratic Party will take control of Congress," Antonio Di Giacomo, a senior market analyst at brokerage XS.com, said, adding that trade relations between the two economies could improve after that.
Among other currencies, the Chilean peso
weakened 1.7% and was within 3% of a record low. Peru's sol
The countries are reliant on copper export revenues and the recent slide in prices of the red metal, partially due to the unwinding of the global AI trade, weighed on the currencies.
strengthened 0.5% after reports said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva had authorized a second package of fiscal measures aimed at curbing mandatory spending.

The recovery highlights how hungry investors are for positive fiscal signals, following a broad repricing of Brazilian assets after Lula's election dashed hopes for a more market-friendly administration under his rival.

"Although the administration has proposed measures to contain spending, investors remain skeptical that these will deliver meaningful fiscal consolidation without deeper structural reforms," said analysts at FrontierView, an Oxford Economics company.

Elsewhere, Venezuela's government published its long-awaited macroeconomic framework, laying out a comprehensive picture of the country's shattered economy and debt for the first time in years, a step that could underpin one of the world's largest-ever debt restructurings.
The government expects economic output to more than double in the next five years, to $200.9 billion, while putting total debt at $237.5 billion. The country defaulted on its debt in 2017.

Venezuelan stocks (.IBC) jumped 4.6% to a one-month high and dollar bonds maturing in 2038 (USP17625AB3=1M) gained over 6 cents on the dollar, while legacy bonds that matured in 2018 (USP9395PAA9=1M) and 2019 (USP97475AN0=1M) rose 3 and 6 cents, respectively.
Equities in Colombia <.COLCAP>, Peru <.MXNUAMPESCPGPE> and Chile <.MMXIPSAGC> were lower.
